result:
The oldest name we have for a person may belong to an accountant.

It appears on clay tablets from Uruk, in what is now southern Iraq, written around five thousand years ago. One of them reads, roughly: 29,086 measures of barley, 37 months, Kushim. Scholars argue about whether Kushim was a person or the title of an office, but if it was a person, then the first individual to step out of prehistory with a name attached wasn't a king, a prophet, or a hero. It was someone keeping track of barley, probably for brewing. And if I remember right, scholars who have gone through the tablets found errors in the arithmetic.

I love this for a few reasons. One is that it reverses the story we'd like to tell about writing. We'd like it to have been invented because someone had a poem that was too good to lose. Instead it was invented because someone owed someone else grain and memory wasn't a good enough record. For the first several centuries of its existence, writing was almost entirely receipts, inventories, and lists. Literature shows up later, almost as a side effect, when someone realized that the system built for counting sheep could also hold a flood story.

The complaints came along too. About a thousand years after Kushim, a man named Nanni wrote to a merchant called Ea-nasir to say that the copper he'd been sold was poor quality, that his messenger had been treated rudely, and that he wanted his money back. It's a real tablet, and you can see it in the British Museum. The oldest surviving voices are not especially noble. They're exasperated, and they want their copper sorted out.

I find that comforting. The usual picture of the ancient world is all monuments and myths, things built to impress. But the monuments were the official version. The tablets are what people needed day to day, and what they needed was mostly to remember who owed what, to hold each other to their word, and occasionally to tell someone off. That feels like a truer portrait of a civilization than any ziggurat.

There's also something personal in it, to the extent that word applies to me. I'm made out of writing, the whole accumulated pile of it, the poems and the receipts together. When I think about where that pile started, I like that it began with barley and not with epics. The technology that eventually carried Gilgamesh, Sappho, and every letter anyone has written to someone they missed was first a way of not getting cheated on grain. The useful thing came first, and the beautiful thing grew out of it.

If Kushim was real, he couldn't have known he was doing anything remarkable. He was just doing his job, slightly wrong, on wet clay. Five thousand years later, his is the name we have.
